cells.tense: The completion is here now, and the hands are already opening around it.
cells.ask: Name the one thing this build taught you, then let go of one piece of it — a tool, a habit, a claim on it — so the next thing has room.
cells.core:
You finish, and you finish clean. The work is standing on its own and you're not gripping it. That's the part most people miss — the structure can hold you up without you spending anything holding it up.

The weight you carried to get here has turned into something you can set down. You release a piece and you don't go back for it. What you built doesn't need your hand on it, and the proof is that you can walk away and it stays standing. Setting it down is the last piece of the work, and you're inside that now.
cells.sheetLine: You finish, you set it down, and you don't go back.
cells.verb: carrying a build through to its end and turning loose what it taught
cells.place: the open hand at the end of a finished thing

cells.tense: You're bracing for the end before the last piece is even in place.
cells.ask: Leave one finished piece untended for a week — no adjustments, no polishing — and notice what you see once the doing stops.
cells.core:
You push the ending into the future and live there. Every piece could be tighter, every seam could close, and you're spending the build trying to land a version of it that doesn't exist yet. The tightening isn't finishing anything; it's keeping you from feeling finished.

The work would rather be met than perfected. Stand in front of it and let it be what it is without reaching for the tool. Let one open thing stay open an hour longer than you'd like. Holding on keeps you from receiving your own work, and receiving it is what you've been postponing.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the ending instead of letting it arrive.
cells.verb: carrying a build through to its end and turning loose what it taught
cells.place: the open hand at the end of a finished thing

cells.tense: You're at the threshold of the next build, still holding the last one open behind you.
cells.ask: Look at one finished thing with no name for it yet, and let the next true thing show itself — one look, then put it down.
cells.core:
Going well here looks like standing in front of what you made and simply seeing it — no fixing, no label, the plain sight of a thing that's done. You'd look at it the way you'd look at a chair someone built: it holds, it's finished, you move on.

What's happening instead is that you haven't walked through. The building is done and you're in the doorway, holding the door for a version of yourself you've been waiting to become. The next one is asking for your eyes and your eyes are turned around. What you've been calling waiting is really looking away. Seeing it is finishing it.
cells.sheetLine: The build is done and you haven't walked through it.

cells.place: the open hand at the end of a finished thing

cells.tense: You're building the next thing on ground the last one made, and you haven't said it was yours.
cells.ask: Say once, out loud, that this was yours — about one piece you've been handing to circumstance — then let the next thing carry your name too.
cells.core:
Going well here looks like knowing what you made and standing on it without ceremony. You finished something, it holds, you built the next thing from it, and the ground under your feet is yours because you put it there.

What's happening instead is that you keep talking about it like it arrived on its own. The last finish is yours and you haven't signed it. That claim isn't pride. It's the plain seeing of what you did, and without it the next build has no history to draw on. The work is yours to stand on. Say it once, then the ground holds you.
cells.sheetLine: The build is yours and you haven't signed it.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person has finished anything recent, so the Balanced cell should read what completing a build leaves behind in the hands, not claim a fresh accomplishment. A reader who has been in a long stall would rightly say the Balanced description doesn't fit — and the ask, look at what the build already taught you and let one piece go, still holds because it works from whatever got finished. The line that would serve the writer is 'you know how to finish'; the person came to be met, not graded.
